references.text: The scribes and Pharisees were already filled with rage against Jesus from early in his ministry and made plans against him. See [ref:Luk 6:11|Luke 6:11].
Jesus' harsh speech against the legal experts in [ref:Luk 11:45-46|Luke 11:45-46] is the immediate context that provoked the hostile reaction of the scribes and Pharisees.
Jesus had just pronounced a series of woes upon the legal experts ([ref:Luk 11:47-52|Luke 11:47-52]), which led to the intense opposition described here.
The Pharisees and Herodians tried to trap Jesus in his words, parallel to the trap that the scribes and Pharisees attempt to set up here. See [ref:Mark 12:13|Mark 12:13].
The Pharisees plotted how they could catch Jesus in his words ([ref:Matt 22:15|Matthew 22:15]), a strategy similar to the one described in this verse.
The scribes and chief priests sent spies to catch Jesus in something he said, so that they could hand him over to the authorities. See [ref:Luk 20:20|Luke 20:20].

The psalmist describes enemies who gather together, lie in wait, and watch his steps to take his life—a situation that reflects the persecution of Jesus by the scribes and Pharisees. See [ref:Sal 56:6-7|Psalm 56:6-7].
The scribes and leaders constantly sought to put Jesus to death but could not find a way, because the people held fast to him. See [ref:Luk 19:47-48|Luke 19:47-48].

Isaiah speaks of those who set traps for the one who upholds justice and with empty words seek to bring down the righteous—a prophetic parallel to the scribes' attempt to trap Jesus in his words. See [ref:Jes 29:21|Isaiah 29:21].

Jeremiah describes enemies who plotted against the prophet and said they would strike him with their tongue—a parallel to the opponents' attempt to provoke Jesus into saying something they could use against him. See [ref:Jer 18:18|Jeremiah 18:18].
